title: ChatGPT and the public moment
text:
CHAPTER 19. LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
SECTION 19.2. CHATGPT AND THE PUBLIC MOMENT

On 30 November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT as a free "research preview": a chat interface to a language model fine-tuned for dialogue with the RLHF methods of Section 19.1. Its underlying technology was not new to researchers; models of similar capability had been available through OpenAI's API for months. Yet ChatGPT became one of the fastest-adopted consumer products ever and moved AI, in a few weeks, from a technical field into a subject of everyday conversation, business strategy and government policy. This section describes what ChatGPT was, why it spread so fast, how industry and governments reacted, and what the public learned about the strengths and weaknesses of large language models (LLMs).

1. What ChatGPT was

OpenAI's announcement described a model trained to interact conversationally: to answer follow-up questions, admit mistakes, challenge incorrect premises and reject inappropriate requests. It was a sibling of InstructGPT, fine-tuned from a model in the "GPT-3.5" series (models trained on a mix of text and code that finished training in early 2022), with RLHF using dialogue data. Human trainers wrote conversations playing both user and assistant, and ranked alternative model responses to train the reward model, which was then used to fine-tune the policy with PPO, as in Section 19.1.

From a technical point of view, the key ingredients were:

  - A large pretrained transformer decoder (Section 18.3), with its parameters and training data not disclosed.
  - Instruction tuning and RLHF for helpful, conversational behavior and some refusals of harmful requests.
  - A dialogue format: the whole conversation is fed back into the model as context at each turn, so it appears to "remember" the conversation (within its context window).
  - A free, simple web interface with no API key or programming needed.

The last point mattered as much as the others. GPT-3 had required developers and prompts written in a particular style; ChatGPT let anyone simply ask.

2. The speed of adoption

ChatGPT reached one million users within about five days, according to OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman, and an estimated 100 million monthly active users about two months after launch, according to an analysis reported by Reuters in early 2023, which made it, by that estimate, the fastest-growing consumer application up to that time. Usage kept rising: by February 2026, OpenAI reportedly had around 900 million weekly users. In February 2023, OpenAI launched a paid subscription, ChatGPT Plus.

People used it for writing and editing emails, summarizing documents, explaining concepts, translating, brainstorming and, very widely, programming help. Students used it for homework, creating an immediate crisis for schools and universities over essays and take-home assessments; some school systems initially blocked it, and many later moved toward allowing it with rules. A February 2023 study reported that ChatGPT performed at or near the passing threshold on the United States Medical Licensing Examination, one of many studies testing it on professional exams.

3. Industry reaction: the AI race

The release triggered intense competition:

  - Microsoft, which had invested in OpenAI since 2019, announced on 23 January 2023 an additional multiyear investment widely reported as about 10 billion US dollars, and on 7 February 2023 launched a new Bing search engine with a GPT-based chat assistant (later integrated into products under the Copilot brand).
  - Google, whose researchers had invented the transformer and which had built large dialogue models (LaMDA, 2021-2022) but had not released them widely, announced its chatbot Bard on 6 February 2023. An error in a promotional demonstration, a wrong statement about the James Webb Space Telescope, was widely reported, and Alphabet's share price fell sharply. Bard was later rebranded Gemini, after Google DeepMind's model family (Google merged its Brain team and DeepMind in April 2023).
  - On 14 March 2023, OpenAI released GPT-4 (Section 19.3), which accepted images as well as text. Its technical report gave results on professional and academic exams, such as a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10 percent of test takers (a figure later re-examined by other researchers, who found lower percentiles under other comparisons), but disclosed no details of model size, data or training compute, citing competition and safety.
  - Anthropic (founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers including Dario and Daniela Amodei) released Claude in March 2023. Many other companies and startups released chat assistants in 2023-2024.
  - Meta released LLaMA in February 2023 to researchers; its weights soon leaked publicly, and Meta then released Llama 2 (July 2023) with a license permitting commercial use. This started a strong "open-weight" ecosystem, joined by Mistral (France), Alibaba's Qwen, and DeepSeek (China), whose models in 2024-2025 approached the best closed models at much lower reported training costs (Section 19.3).
  - Demand for GPUs (Chapter 15) exploded. NVIDIA's data-center revenue grew several-fold, and its market value passed 1 trillion US dollars in 2023 and later became, for periods, the largest of any company in the world. Access to GPUs became a strategic concern for companies and governments (Section 20.1).

4. What people discovered: strengths

Large audiences discovered that LLMs could:

  - Write fluent, well-organized text in many styles and languages, including smaller languages with limited data, at varying quality.
  - Explain and transform: summarize, rewrite for a different audience, translate, convert between formats (for example, prose to a table or code).
  - Write and debug code; programming assistance became one of the most valuable uses, and a study by GitHub and Microsoft researchers on an earlier coding assistant reported developers finishing a controlled task faster with it.
  - Answer a very wide range of questions at the level of a well-read generalist.

5. What people discovered: weaknesses

The same users found the limits quickly:

  - Hallucination: LLMs generate fluent but false statements, including invented citations, quotes and facts, presented with confidence. They model what text is likely, not what is true. In a well-known case, in 2023, lawyers in New York were sanctioned for filing a brief containing nonexistent court cases generated by ChatGPT. Grounding answers in retrieved documents (retrieval-augmented generation, RAG; Patrick Lewis and colleagues, 2020) and tool use (Section 19.3) reduce but do not eliminate the problem.
  - Reasoning errors: early ChatGPT made mistakes in arithmetic, counting and multi-step logic, and could be argued into wrong answers.
  - Knowledge cutoff: a model knows only its training data up to some date, unless connected to search.
  - Jailbreaks and prompt injection: users found prompts that bypassed safety training (role-play scenarios such as "DAN," "do anything now"); and text hidden in web pages or documents could hijack a model that reads them, a security problem for systems that act on behalf of users.
  - Bias and inconsistency: outputs reflected biases in training data and could change with small changes in wording.
  - Privacy and copyright: models were trained on huge amounts of web text, books and code, often without permission. Many lawsuits followed, including authors' suits and The New York Times' suit against OpenAI and Microsoft (December 2023), and several of these cases continued in the courts for years, making the legal status of training on copyrighted material a central open question.

6. Governments and public debate

The public moment also became a policy moment:

  - At the end of March 2023, Italy's data protection authority temporarily banned ChatGPT over privacy concerns; it became available again at the end of April 2023, after OpenAI made changes.
  - On 22 March 2023, the Future of Life Institute published an open letter calling for a pause of at least six months in training AI systems more powerful than GPT-4; it gathered many signatures, including well-known researchers and technology figures, but no such pause took place.
  - In May 2023, Geoffrey Hinton announced that he had left Google so he could speak freely about AI risks. On 30 May 2023, the Center for AI Safety published a one-sentence statement, signed by many leading researchers and executives: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."
  - Other researchers argued that focusing on hypothetical extinction risks distracted from present harms such as bias, misinformation, labor exploitation in data labeling, and concentration of power.
  - Governments responded: the United Kingdom hosted an AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park in November 2023; the United States issued an executive order on AI in October 2023 (later rescinded in January 2025); and the European Union's AI Act, a risk-based law, entered into force on 1 August 2024, with obligations phased in over the following years. China introduced rules for generative AI services in 2023.
  - Labor: the 2023 Hollywood writers' strike included protections around AI in its settlement, and economists began to study effects on jobs in writing, customer support, translation and programming.

7. Recognition

In October 2024, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton "for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks," and half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind for protein structure prediction (AlphaFold), the other half to David Baker for computational protein design. Seventy years after the perceptron (Chapter 10), neural network research was recognized at the highest level of science.

8. Why this moment, and not earlier?

Several factors came together in late 2022:

  - Capability crossed a threshold of usefulness for ordinary tasks, the result of scale (Section 18.3) plus RLHF (Section 19.1).
  - A chat interface fitted how people already communicate, and required no technical skill.
  - Free access and word of mouth, amplified by social media screenshots, spread it quickly.
  - Cloud infrastructure (Microsoft Azure) could serve millions of users, though at high cost; OpenAI's leaders publicly described the computing costs as very large.

Researchers knew that the underlying methods had been building since 2017, but for most of the world AI arrived suddenly. As with the "AI summers" of earlier decades (Chapters 9 and 12), expectations rose very quickly, raising the question of whether a correction would follow; this time the commercial use of the technology was much broader than in any earlier wave.

9. Summary

  - ChatGPT (30 November 2022) was a GPT-3.5 model fine-tuned for dialogue with RLHF and offered free through a simple chat interface.
  - It reached about 1 million users in five days and an estimated 100 million monthly users in about two months.
  - It triggered an industry race: Microsoft's investment and Bing chat, Google's Bard (later Gemini), GPT-4 (March 2023), Claude, open-weight models such as LLaMA, and a surge in GPU demand.
  - The public discovered both broad usefulness (writing, explanation, coding) and serious weaknesses (hallucination, jailbreaks, bias, copyright questions).
  - Governments and researchers debated risks; the EU AI Act entered into force in August 2024; Hopfield and Hinton received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
